params.question: What is the key difference between stochastic and deterministic effects of ionising radiation?

answers.text: Stochastic effects appear immediately after exposure, while deterministic effects are delayed by decades

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: It is actually the reverse. Stochastic effects such as cancer appear late, often decades after exposure. Deterministic effects like skin burns and cataracts appear early, once the threshold dose is exceeded.

answers.text: Stochastic effects have no threshold dose and increase in probability with dose, while deterministic effects occur only above a threshold and increase in severity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Stochastic effects follow the linear no-threshold model — any dose carries some non-zero risk, and higher doses raise the probability (not severity) of harm. Deterministic effects require a threshold dose to appear, and severity then rises with increasing dose.

answers.text: Stochastic effects only cause cancer, while deterministic effects only cause genetic mutations

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Stochastic effects include both carcinogenesis and hereditary (genetic) effects. Deterministic effects include tissue reactions such as skin burns, hair loss, cataracts, and sterility — not genetic mutations.

answers.text: Deterministic effects are the dominant concern at diagnostic doses because they have no safe threshold

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: It is stochastic effects that lack a threshold and are the dominant concern at diagnostic dose levels. Deterministic effects only appear above a threshold dose, which is rarely reached in routine diagnostic imaging.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the two categories. Stochastic effects have NO threshold — any dose raises the probability of harm (not severity). Deterministic effects occur ONLY above a threshold, and their severity then increases with dose. This distinction underpins all radiation protection.

Excellent. The threshold distinction is the defining feature: stochastic effects (cancer, hereditary changes) follow the linear no-threshold model, while deterministic effects (burns, cataracts, sterility) require a threshold dose before they appear.

interactions.label: A radiation worker's dosimeter report expresses cumulative dose in millisieverts

params.question: A radiation worker's dosimeter report expresses cumulative dose in millisieverts rather than milligrays. Why is the Sievert more appropriate for radiation protection purposes?

answers.text: The Gray can only measure doses from X-rays, not from gamma rays

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The Gray measures absorbed dose from any type of ionising radiation. It is insufficient for protection because it does not account for the differing biological effects of different radiation types and tissue sensitivities.

answers.text: The Sievert weights the absorbed dose by both the type of radiation and the sensitivity of the tissue exposed, reflecting actual biological risk

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The Sievert converts the purely physical measurement (Gray) into an effective dose that captures biological harm. This is why occupational dose limits and imaging-study comparisons use millisieverts.

answers.text: Millisieverts are always numerically larger than milligrays, making small doses easier to detect on the badge

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The numerical relationship between Gray and Sievert depends on the radiation and tissue weighting factors applied. The Sievert's value lies in reflecting biological risk, not in producing a larger number.

answers.text: The Sievert measures the total duration of exposure rather than the energy deposited

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The Sievert does not measure time. It takes the absorbed energy (Gray) and weights it by radiation type and tissue sensitivity to yield effective dose — a measure of biological risk, not exposure duration.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the memory aid from the video: Gray measures the physics (energy going in), Sievert measures the risk (biological harm coming out). The Sievert incorporates weighting for radiation type and tissue sensitivity, which is why dose limits and imaging comparisons always use millisieverts.

Well done. Gray measures the physics — energy deposited per kilogram of tissue. Sievert measures the risk — biological harm — by weighting for radiation type and tissue sensitivity. Remember: Gray = energy in, Sievert = risk out.

interactions.label: The occupational dose limit of 20 millisieverts per year also applies as a cap o

params.question: The occupational dose limit of 20 millisieverts per year also applies as a cap on the radiation dose a patient may receive from diagnostic imaging.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This is false. The 20 mSv/year limit applies to occupationally exposed workers, and 1 mSv/year to the general public. Patients have no diagnostic dose cap. Their protection comes from two of the three principles: justification (ensuring the scan provides net benefit) and optimisation (keeping the dose as low as reasonably achievable).
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this is false. The 20 mSv/year limit applies to occupationally exposed workers (1 mSv/year for the general public), but NOT to patients undergoing diagnostic imaging. Patient protection relies entirely on justification (does this scan change management?) and optimisation (ALARA), not on a numerical dose ceiling.

interactions.label: A surgical registrar relies solely on his lead apron during prolonged fluoroscop

params.question: A surgical registrar relies solely on his lead apron during prolonged fluoroscopy cases. Which components of the ALARA triad is he neglecting?

answers.text: He needs a thicker lead apron of at least 1.0 mm lead equivalent to achieve adequate shielding

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Standard lead aprons of 0.25 to 0.5 mm lead equivalent provide adequate shielding. The registrar's problem is not the apron's thickness but his neglect of the other two ALARA components — minimising beam-on time and maximising distance from the source.

answers.text: He is addressing shielding but neglecting time reduction and distance, which are equally essential components of ALARA

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. ALARA rests on three legs: time, distance, and shielding. Minimising screening time and stepping back to exploit the inverse-square law (double the distance reduces dose to one quarter) are equally critical. Relying on shielding alone is the most common real-world protection failure.

answers.text: He should apply for a dose-limit exemption from AERB before performing fluoroscopy-guided procedures

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: No such exemption exists. AERB enforces dose limits and facility compliance under the Atomic Energy Act. The solution is better technique — shorter screening time, greater distance, and shielding applied together — not a regulatory workaround.

answers.text: He should avoid being present in the fluoroscopy room entirely during screening

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Clinicians often must be present during fluoroscopy-guided procedures. The correct approach is applying all three ALARA legs simultaneously: keeping beam-on time minimal, stepping back whenever possible to exploit the inverse-square law, and wearing appropriate shielding.

overallFeedback.feedback: ALARA is not a single measure but a triad: time (minimise beam-on duration), distance (inverse-square law — double the distance, quarter the dose), and shielding (lead apron, thyroid shield, lead glasses). Relying on any one leg alone is incomplete and is the most common protection failure in clinical practice.

Excellent. A lead apron addresses only shielding. Without also minimising beam-on time and maximising distance (inverse-square law), dose accumulates unnecessarily. All three ALARA legs must be applied together, every time.
